<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 0:35–1:15 · Warm-up march

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>0:35</td><td>Chang</td><td>Ankle pumps first if you've been sitting. Stand slowly. Hand on the counter.</td><td>Warm-up march</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:54</td><td>Chang</td><td>March. Easy rhythm. Breathe steady.</td><td>Easier: Sit and march</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Stand tall. Knee up, foot down softly. **Easier:** Sit and do the seated march. **Harder:** Lift knees higher, march faster, or let one hand hover above the counter.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 1:15–1:45 · Easy sit-to-stands

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>1:15</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chair against the wall. Five easy ones.</td><td>Easy sit-to-stands</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:30</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you stand.</td><td>Easier: Higher seat, hands on thighs</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Nose over toes. Knees point the same way as your toes. Don't let them cave inward. Sit down slow. Two or three seconds. **Easier:** Put a firm cushion or folded blanket on the seat to make it higher, or push up with your hands on your thighs or on chair arms. **Harder:** Arms crossed, lower for a slow count of three, and pause one second just above the seat before touching down. Later: hold a gallon jug of water at your chest.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 1:45–3:45 · Legs

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>1:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Legs</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:07</td><td>Chang</td><td>Cross your arms over your chest, or rest your hands on your thighs.</td><td>Easier: Higher seat, hands on thighs</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:26</td><td>Chang</td><td>Nose over toes.</td><td>Advanced (Iron): not your starting point</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:39</td><td>Chang</td><td>One... two... breathe out... three... slow down... four.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>2:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Knees point the same way as your toes. Don't let them cave inward.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>3:04</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you stand. Breathe in as you sit.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Nose over toes. Knees point the same way as your toes. Don't let them cave inward. Sit down slow. Two or three seconds. **Easier:** Put a firm cushion or folded blanket on the seat to make it higher, or push up with your hands on your thighs or on chair arms. **Harder:** Arms crossed, lower for a slow count of three, and pause one second just above the seat before touching down. Later: hold a gallon jug of water at your chest.

**Safety callouts:** Stop the fast part if you feel dizzy when you stand. Go back to normal speed. Advanced. Only if your knees feel good with step-ups.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 3:45–5:15 · Push

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>3:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Push</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:02</td><td>Chang</td><td>Lower your chest toward the counter edge.</td><td>Easier: Wall push-ups</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:16</td><td>Chang</td><td>Straight line from head to heels.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>4:25</td><td>Chang</td><td>One... two... breathe out... three... slow down... four.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>4:31</td><td>Chang</td><td>Squeeze your buttocks so your hips don't sag.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>4:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you push up.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Straight line from head to heels. Squeeze your buttocks so your hips don't sag. **Easier:** Wall push-ups. **Harder:** Lower slowly for three seconds. Later (Iron track): a sturdy low bench or bottom stair, only if the counter version is easy for 12 reps.

**Safety callouts:** Wrist pain? Make fists or hold the counter edge instead of flat palms.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 5:15–6:25 · Band row

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>5:15</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit or stand with the chair behind you. Check the band first.</td><td>Band row</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:29</td><td>Chang</td><td>Pull your elbows back past your ribs.</td><td>Easier: Closer to the door, or towel</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:40</td><td>Chang</td><td>Elbows close to your body.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:46</td><td>Chang</td><td>One... two... breathe out... three... slow down... four.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:51</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tall chest, shoulders down.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>6:02</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you pull.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Elbows close to your body. Tall chest, shoulders down. **Easier:** Sit closer to the door so the band is slacker, or do the towel pull-apart. **Harder:** Scoot back for more tension, or pause 2 seconds with elbows back.

**Safety callouts:** Check the band for nicks before every use. Door must open away from you and be locked.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 6:25–7:45 · Floor practice

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>6:25</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chair beside you. Towel down. Someone home.</td><td>Floor practice</td></tr>
<tr><td>6:44</td><td>Chang</td><td>Kneel, then rise through the front foot. Hands on the chair.</td><td>Easier: Half-kneel only, or chair stands</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you push up. Stand still a moment.</td><td>Only with a sturdy chair and someone home</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:16</td><td>Chang</td><td>New knee or dizziness: chair stands instead.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Hands on the chair the whole time. Slow down. Up is a push, not a jump. **Easier:** Only the first step: lower into a half-kneel on the towel and come back up, holding the chair. Or skip the floor and do sit-to-stands. **Harder:** Iron: from kneeling, sit down onto the floor beside the chair, then roll to your knees and rise with the chair. Only with someone home.

**Safety callouts:** Only try the floor with a sturdy chair or sofa next to you and someone home. Recent hip or knee replacement, or severe knee arthritis: follow your surgeon's or physical therapist's guidance first. New knee? Kneeling may not be allowed yet. Ask your surgeon. Sit a moment before you stand, then stand slowly while holding something steady.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 7:45–8:30 · Heel raises

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>7:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Heel raises</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:55</td><td>Chang</td><td>Rise up onto the balls of your feet, as high as is comfortable.</td><td>Easier: Seated, or rise halfway</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:02</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tall like someone is pulling a string on top of your head.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:05</td><td>Chang</td><td>One... two... breathe out... three... slow down... four.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:09</td><td>Chang</td><td>Weight over the big toe and second toe, not rolling out.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:16</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you rise.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Tall like someone is pulling a string on top of your head. Weight over the big toe and second toe, not rolling out. **Easier:** Sit in your chair and raise your heels from there, or hold the counter with both hands and rise only halfway. **Harder:** One hand on the counter. Later: one leg at a time, with both hands on the counter.

**Safety callouts:** Calf cramps are common at first. Stretch and walk them out. One calf that is swollen, red and painful is not a cramp: that is for your doctor, today.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 8:30–9:15 · Calf stretch

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>8:30</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Calf stretch</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:40</td><td>Chang</td><td>Bend the front knee and lean gently toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the back calf.</td><td>Easier: Smaller step back</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:47</td><td>Chang</td><td>Back heel stays down.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:54</td><td>Chang</td><td>Toes point forward.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>9:01</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly through the stretch.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Back heel stays down. Toes point forward. **Easier:** Smaller step back. **Harder:** Bigger step back, or bend the back knee slightly to reach the lower calf.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 9:15–9:45 · Cool-down breathing

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>9:15</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit down. Two sniffs in through the nose. One long sigh out.</td><td>Cool-down breathing</td></tr>
<tr><td>9:30</td><td>Chang</td><td>No holding.</td><td>Easier: Just slow nose breathing</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Two sniffs in, one long sigh out. No holding at any point. **Easier:** Just breathe slowly through your nose, making the out-breath a little longer. **Harder:** Build up to 5 minutes.

**Safety callouts:** If you feel light-headed, return to normal breathing.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 9:45–10:10 · Close

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>9:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Month two. Strong is a habit.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>9:58</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tomorrow: mobility, then your full retest in the app.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

</div>

|---|---|---|---|---|

## Script

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 0:00–0:35 · Welcome

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 0:35–1:05 · Ankle pumps

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>0:35</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>Ankle pumps</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:42</td><td>Chang</td><td>Point your toes away, then pull them toward you. That's one pump.</td><td>Easier: Smaller movements</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:47</td><td>Chang</td><td>Big, slow movements.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>0:52</td><td>Chang</td><td>Feel your calves work.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>0:57</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Big, slow movements. Feel your calves work. **Easier:** Smaller movements. **Harder:** Lift one foot off the floor while you circle.

**Safety callouts:** Great before you stand up from sitting or lying. Sit a moment before you stand, then stand slowly while holding something steady.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 1:05–1:35 · Shoulder rolls

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>1:05</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>Shoulder rolls</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:12</td><td>Chang</td><td>Lift your shoulders up toward your ears.</td><td>Easier: Just shrug and let go</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:17</td><td>Chang</td><td>Big, slow circles, backward.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>1:22</td><td>Chang</td><td>Let your arms hang heavy.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>1:27</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe in as you lift, out as you roll down.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Big, slow circles, backward. Let your arms hang heavy. **Easier:** Just shrug up and let go. **Harder:** Add arm circles: small circles out to the sides, forward and back.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 1:35–2:15 · Chest lift

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>1:35</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>Chest lift</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:44</td><td>Chang</td><td>Lift your chest up toward the ceiling, growing tall.</td><td>Easier: Smaller lift</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:50</td><td>Chang</td><td>Grow tall.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>1:57</td><td>Chang</td><td>Look straight ahead, not up.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>2:03</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe in as you lift, out as you relax.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Grow tall. Look straight ahead, not up. **Easier:** Smaller lift. **Harder:** Hold three seconds at the top.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 2:15–3:00 · Seated hinge

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>2:15</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>Seated hinge</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:25</td><td>Chang</td><td>Keep your back long and tip your chest forward from the hips, sliding your hands toward your knees.</td><td>Easier: Smaller tip forward</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:32</td><td>Chang</td><td>Long back, proud chest.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>2:39</td><td>Chang</td><td>Bend at the hips, not the belly.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>2:46</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you sit tall.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Long back, proud chest. Bend at the hips, not the belly. **Easier:** A smaller tip forward. **Harder:** Hold a water bottle against your chest.

**Safety callouts:** Osteoporosis: this is the safe bending pattern. Keep the back long, never curl.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 3:00–3:55 · Standing hip-front stretch

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>3:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Standing hip-front stretch</td></tr>
<tr><td>3:11</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tuck your tailbone under slightly and squeeze the buttock of the back leg.</td><td>Easier: Smaller step, both hands down</td></tr>
<tr><td>3:20</td><td>Chang</td><td>Stay tall. Don't arch your back.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>3:29</td><td>Chang</td><td>Small movement, big squeeze.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>3:38</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Stay tall. Don't arch your back. Small movement, big squeeze. **Easier:** Smaller step. **Harder:** Reach the arm on the back-leg side up toward the ceiling, to comfortable height.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 3:55–4:40 · Calf stretch

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>3:55</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Calf stretch</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:05</td><td>Chang</td><td>Bend the front knee and lean gently toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the back calf.</td><td>Easier: Smaller step back</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:12</td><td>Chang</td><td>Back heel stays down.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>4:19</td><td>Chang</td><td>Toes point forward.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>4:26</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly through the stretch.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Back heel stays down. Toes point forward. **Easier:** Smaller step back. **Harder:** Bigger step back, or bend the back knee slightly to reach the lower calf.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 4:40–5:20 · Weight shifts

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>4:40</td><td>Chang</td><td>Hand on the counter. Chair behind you.</td><td>Weight shifts</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:49</td><td>Chang</td><td>Slowly shift your weight to your right foot. Pause.</td><td>Easier: Do it seated</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:55</td><td>Chang</td><td>Move from your ankles and hips, like a tree swaying.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:02</td><td>Chang</td><td>Feet stay flat on the floor.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:08</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Move from your ankles and hips, like a tree swaying. Feet stay flat on the floor. **Easier:** Do it seated: shift your weight side to side on the chair. **Harder:** Make the shifts bigger, or let one hand hover.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 5:20–6:05 · Wall slides

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>5:20</td><td>Chang</td><td>Wall in front of you or behind you. Chair nearby.</td><td>Wall slides</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:30</td><td>Chang</td><td>Slide your arms up the wall only as far as comfortable.</td><td>Easier: Walk fingertips up the wall</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:37</td><td>Chang</td><td>Ribs down.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:44</td><td>Chang</td><td>Slow and smooth.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>5:51</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe in as you slide up, out as you slide down.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Ribs down. Slow and smooth. **Easier:** Face the wall and walk your fingertips up it instead. **Harder:** Hold for two seconds at the top.

**Safety callouts:** Shoulder pain or a known rotator cuff problem? Only lift to a comfortable height, or skip it.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 6:05–6:55 · Seated hamstring stretch

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>6:05</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>Seated hamstring stretch</td></tr>
<tr><td>6:16</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall, hands on your bent knee.</td><td>Easier: Lean only an inch</td></tr>
<tr><td>6:24</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chest proud. Bend from the hips, not the back.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>6:32</td><td>Chang</td><td>A gentle stretch is enough.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>6:40</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe slowly.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Chest proud. Bend from the hips, not the back. A gentle stretch is enough. **Easier:** Lean only an inch or two. **Harder:** Pull your toes toward you a little more.

**Safety callouts:** Osteoporosis or a past spine fracture: keep the back long. Never curl down toward your toes.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 6:55–7:55 · 4-6 breathing

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>6:55</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Chair against the wall.</td><td>4-6 breathing</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:07</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe in through your nose for a count of 4.</td><td>Easier: In for 3, out for 4</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:17</td><td>Chang</td><td>Belly rises first.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>7:26</td><td>Chang</td><td>Soft shoulders.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>7:36</td><td>Chang</td><td>In for 4, out for 6. That is about 6 breaths a minute. No holds.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Belly rises first. Soft shoulders. **Easier:** In for 3, out for 4. **Harder:** Continue for 5 minutes.

**Safety callouts:** If you feel light-headed, go back to normal breathing.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 7:55–8:25 · Close

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>7:55</td><td>Chang</td><td>Loose and ready. Water. Rest ten minutes.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:06</td><td>Chang</td><td>Then the retest. Same chair, same shoes, same way as day one.</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>8:14</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tell me your Strength Age.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

# Guided retest (day 30, 60, 90…): Your Strength Age retest

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guided retest | 10:25 | SET-KITCHEN | C-TRAIN-B | Chang |

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">On screen the whole session:</span> the "AI character" corner tag. In the first 30 seconds and before each hard block: "Stop if chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain."

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Gentle-day swaps (the sore knee / sore back / low energy button):</span> **Sore knee:** Skip the step test and the Up and Go today; do them another day. **Sore back:** Skip the sit-and-reach. **Low energy:** Do the chair stand and balance only; finish the rest tomorrow.
</div>

## Script

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 0:00–0:45 · Welcome

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>0:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>Retest day. Same chair, same shoes, same time of day as last time.</td><td>Strength Age retest</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:12</td><td>Chang</td><td>Six tests. About twelve minutes with rests. A helper is welcome.</td><td>Not a medical test</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:21</td><td>Chang</td><td>These are fitness checks from senior fitness research. Not a medical test.</td><td>Stop if chest pain or dizziness</td></tr>
<tr><td>0:30</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chest pain, dizziness, unusual breathlessness: stop, and call your doctor.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 0:45–2:00 · Test 1: 30-second chair stand

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>0:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chair against the wall. Sit in the middle. Arms crossed.</td><td>Test 1: 30-second chair stand</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:03</td><td>Chang</td><td>Three, two, one, go. All the way up, all the way down.</td><td>Easier: Higher seat, hands on thighs</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:18</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you stand. Ten seconds left.</td><td>Count full stands</td></tr>
<tr><td>1:33</td><td>Chang</td><td>Stop. Enter your number.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Nose over toes. Knees point the same way as your toes. Don't let them cave inward. Sit down slow. Two or three seconds. **Easier:** Put a firm cushion or folded blanket on the seat to make it higher, or push up with your hands on your thighs or on chair arms. **Harder:** Arms crossed, lower for a slow count of three, and pause one second just above the seat before touching down. Later: hold a gallon jug of water at your chest.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 2:00–3:45 · Test 2: four-stage balance

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>2:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>At the counter. Hand hovering just above it. Helper beside you.</td><td>Test 2: four-stage balance</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:24</td><td>Chang</td><td>Feet together, ten seconds. Then half step. Then heel to toe. Then one foot.</td><td>Easier: Half-step, both hands down</td></tr>
<tr><td>2:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Touch the counter or move your feet, and that stage is over. Breathe.</td><td>Stop at the first stage you can't hold</td></tr>
<tr><td>3:06</td><td>Chang</td><td>Enter the last stage you held for ten seconds.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Eyes on something still at eye level. Soft knees. Tall head. **Easier:** Half-step stance: front foot's heel beside the big toe of the back foot. Both hands on the counter. **Harder:** Lift one hand to hover just above the counter. Later: both hands hovering.

**Safety callouts:** Balance drills always start with support. Hands hover, they don't wander away from the counter.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 3:45–4:45 · Test 3: arm curl

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>3:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Sit tall. Weight in your stronger hand. Same weight as last time.</td><td>Test 3: arm curl</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:04</td><td>Chang</td><td>Go. Full curls. Elbow by your side.</td><td>Easier: One arm, or empty bottles</td></tr>
<tr><td>4:20</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you curl. Stop. Enter your number.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Elbows stay by your sides. No swinging. **Easier:** One arm at a time, or empty bottles. **Harder:** Heavier: a half-gallon jug (about 4 pounds), then a full gallon jug (about 8 pounds), one at a time.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 4:45–7:15 · Test 4: two-minute step test

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>4:45</td><td>Chang</td><td>Tape on the counter halfway between your kneecap and hip bone. Hand on the counter.</td><td>Test 4: two-minute step test</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:12</td><td>Chang</td><td>March, lifting each knee to the tape. Count the right knee.</td><td>Easier: Sit and march</td></tr>
<tr><td>5:36</td><td>Chang</td><td>Slow down or rest any time. The clock keeps running.</td><td>Count right-knee lifts</td></tr>
<tr><td>6:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe. Heart condition or breathless easily? Skip this one until your doctor says okay.</td><td>Skip if breathless easily</td></tr>
<tr><td>6:24</td><td>Chang</td><td>Stop. Keep walking slowly for a minute. Don't sit straight away.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Stand tall. Knee up, foot down softly. **Easier:** Sit and do the seated march. **Harder:** Lift knees higher, march faster, or let one hand hover above the counter.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 7:15–8:25 · Test 5: chair sit-and-reach

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>7:15</td><td>Chang</td><td>Front edge of the chair. One leg straight, heel down.</td><td>Test 5: chair sit-and-reach</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:32</td><td>Chang</td><td>Long back. Hinge forward from the hips. Hold two seconds.</td><td>Easier: Lean only an inch</td></tr>
<tr><td>7:46</td><td>Chang</td><td>Osteoporosis or a past spine fracture: skip this one.</td><td>Osteoporosis: skip this test</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:00</td><td>Chang</td><td>Breathe out as you reach. Measure fingertips to shoe. Enter your best.</td><td></td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Chest proud. Bend from the hips, not the back. A gentle stretch is enough. **Easier:** Lean only an inch or two. **Harder:** Pull your toes toward you a little more.

**Safety callouts:** Osteoporosis or a past spine fracture: keep the back long. Never curl down toward your toes.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 8:25–9:40 · Test 6: Timed Up and Go

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>8:25</td><td>Chang</td><td>Chair against the wall. Tape on the floor ten feet away. Helper with the timer, walking beside you.</td><td>Test 6: Timed Up and Go</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:43</td><td>Chang</td><td>Normal pace. Not a race. Go.</td><td>Easier: Indoors, touching the counter</td></tr>
<tr><td>8:58</td><td>Chang</td><td>Stand, walk to the tape, turn, walk back, sit. Breathe.</td><td>Normal pace, not a race</td></tr>
<tr><td>9:13</td><td>Chang</td><td>Twelve seconds or more? Mention it to your doctor. Balance training is exactly what helps.</td><td>12 s or more: tell your doctor</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

**Cues:** Tall. Eyes ahead, not at your feet. Arms swing naturally. Heel, then toe. **Easier:** Walk indoors: kitchen to front door and back, touching the counter as you pass. Or march seated. **Harder:** Add 1-minute faster stretches, or a gentle hill.

**Safety callouts:** Chest pain, pressure, or unusual breathlessness: stop, sit, and call your doctor. If it doesn't settle in a few minutes, call 911.

</div>

<div class="seg" markdown="1">

### 9:40–10:25 · Your result

<table class="small script"><thead><tr><th>Time</th><th>Who</th><th>Spoken</th><th>On screen</th></tr></thead><tbody>

# Where the numbers come from

Every number Chang says out loud in these scripts traces to one of these entries (EVIDENCE.md). Grade A: Cochrane review, large meta-analysis or guideline. B: single good trial or small meta-analysis. C: observational link, not cause. D: physiology, lab or label data.


<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E01** (grade A). Progressive resistance training in older adults: 121 RCTs, 6,700 people, 2–3×/week. Large effect on strength (SMD 0.84), moderate-to-large effect on getting out of a chair (SMD −0.94), gait speed +0.08 m/s, less osteoarthritis pain. Most side effects were minor soreness or joint pain.

<p class="src">Source: Liu & Latham, Cochrane 2009 — https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD002759_progressive-resistance-strength-training-improving-physical-function-older-adults</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E02** (grade A). NSCA position statement: resistance training is safe and effective for older adults, including frail people. Progress gradually. Train 2–3×/week, 1–3 sets of 6–12 reps at 70–85% 1RM once adapted. Include power (fast lifting intent) and balance.

<p class="src">Source: Fragala et al., J Strength Cond Res 2019 — https://journals.lww.com/nsca-jscr/fulltext/2019/08000/resistance_training_for_older_adults__position.1.aspx</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E07** (grade C). PURE study: 142,861 adults in 17 countries. Every 5 kg lower grip strength was linked with 16% higher all-cause mortality and 17% higher CV mortality. Grip predicted mortality better than systolic blood pressure.

<p class="src">Source: Leong et al., Lancet 2015 — https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(14)62000-6/abstract ; summary https://www.consultant360.com/exclusives/could-grip-strength-predict-all-cause-mortality-risk</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E08** (grade C). Sitting-rising test (sit to the floor and stand up without support; score 0–10, lose 1 point per hand/knee support). 2,002 adults aged 51–80. The lowest scorers (0–2) had 5–6× the death risk of the highest (8–10). Each +1 point was linked with 21% lower mortality.

<p class="src">Source: Brito, Araújo et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2012/2014 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/12/121213085202.htm</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E09** (grade C). 10-second one-leg stance (free foot resting on the back of the other calf, arms at sides, 3 tries). 1,702 people aged 51–75. Failing it was linked with 84% higher all-cause mortality over about 7 years. Failure rates: about 18% at 61–65, about 37% at 66–70, over 50% at 71–75.

<p class="src">Source: Araújo et al., BJSM 2022 — https://www.bristol.ac.uk/news/2022/june/tne-second-one-legged-stance.html</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E10** (grade C). Gait speed and survival: 34,485 adults 65+. 0.8 m/s is around median life expectancy. ≥1.0 m/s was linked with longer-than-expected survival. Under 0.6 m/s means higher risk.

<p class="src">Source: Studenski et al., JAMA 2011 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2011/01/110104161621.htm</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E11** (grade A (tool)). CDC STEADI 30-second chair stand (17-inch chair, arms crossed), used in the CDC's older-adult screening. Below-average scores: men 60–64 <14, 65–69 <12, 70–74 <12, 75–79 <11, 80–84 <10, 85–89 <8, 90–94 <7. Women 60–64 <12, 65–69 <11, 70–74 <10, 75–79 <10, 80–84 <9, 85–89 <8, 90–94 <4. If arms are used to stand, the score is 0.

<p class="src">Source: CDC STEADI — https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-30Sec-508.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E13** (grade A−). Otago Exercise Programme: a home programme of leg strengthening, balance exercises and walking designed for older adults, studied in 7 trials with 1,503 people (mean age 81.6). We use its exercise types and progressions; we make no outcome claim from it.

<p class="src">Source: Thomas et al., Age Ageing 2010 — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK78898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E15** (grade B+). Tai chi vs physical therapy for knee osteoarthritis: 204 adults. Similar improvements in pain and function at 12 weeks, sustained to 52 weeks. Tai chi group had more improvement in depression and quality of life.

<p class="src">Source: Wang et al., Ann Intern Med 2016 — https://www.nccih.nih.gov/research/research-results/study-shows-tai-chi-and-physical-therapy-were-equally-helpful-for-knee-osteoarthritis</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E17** (grade A−). Baduanjin/qigong in older adults: meta-analyses report better sleep quality and fewer depressive symptoms (moderate certainty, heterogeneous trials).

<p class="src">Source: Frontiers Public Health 2026 meta-analysis — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13501274/ ; qigong & sleep meta — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12757222/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E18** (grade B). 111 adults, 5 min/day for 1 month. Cyclic sighing (two inhales through the nose, long slow exhale through the mouth) produced the largest daily improvement in positive mood, more than mindfulness meditation. All breathing groups improved.

<p class="src">Source: Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine 2023 — https://stanmed.stanford.edu/cyclic-sighing-stress-relief/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E19** (grade A− (meta)). Voluntary slow breathing (around 6 breaths/min) increases vagally-mediated heart-rate variability during and after practice.

<p class="src">Source: Laborde et al., Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2022 — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149763422002007</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E20** (grade A). Exercise and resting BP: 270 RCTs, 15,827 people. Isometric training lowered BP the most (−8.24/−4.00 mmHg). Wall squat ranked top for systolic. Aerobic −4.49/−2.53, dynamic resistance −4.55/−3.04. These are average changes over weeks of training, not instant.

<p class="src">Source: Edwards et al., BJSM 2023 — https://bmjgroup.com/static-isometric-exercise-such-as-wall-sits-best-for-lowering-blood-pressure/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E22** (grade C). Daily steps: in adults 60+, mortality benefit plateaued at about 6,000–8,000 steps/day. The top quartiles had 40–53% lower risk than the lowest (about 3,500/day).

<p class="src">Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health 2022 — https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/03/220303112207.htm</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E23** (grade A− (meta)). Light walking after meals (even 2–5 minutes) lowers the post-meal glucose rise compared with sitting.

<p class="src">Source: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35147898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E29** (grade B). LIFTMOR: postmenopausal women with low bone mass did supervised high-intensity resistance plus impact training (2×/week, 8 months). BMD at spine and hip improved and physical function improved. It was supervised and progressed.

<p class="src">Source: Watson et al., JBMR 2018 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28975661/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E30** (grade A). Exercise for chronic low back pain: 249 trials, 24,486 people. Pain about 15 points better (0–100 scale) at 3 months vs no treatment or usual care. Function improved modestly.

<p class="src">Source: Hayden et al., Cochrane 2021 — https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD009790_exercise-treatment-chronic-low-back-pain</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E39** (grade A−). High-velocity "power" training (lift with fast intent, lower slowly) gives functional gains similar to or slightly better than traditional training in older adults, and it is safe when supervised and progressed.

<p class="src">Source: J Physiotherapy 2023 systematic review — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S183695532300053X ; Eur Rev Aging Phys Act 2022 — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s11556-022-00297-x</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E40** (grade A (consensus)). Osteoporosis exercise guidance: do resistance and balance training. Avoid rapid, repeated or loaded spinal flexion (sit-ups, toe-touches with weight) and forceful twisting. Flexion-exercise programs were linked with more vertebral fractures.

<p class="src">Source: Giangregorio et al., "Too Fit To Fracture", Osteoporos Int 2014 — https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00198-014-2881-4 ; Sinaki & Mikkelsen, Arch Phys Med Rehabil 1984</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E41** (grade B (known literature)). Pain-monitoring model: during and after exercise, pain up to about 3/10 (we use a conservative threshold) is acceptable if it settles by the next morning and isn't trending up week to week.

<p class="src">Source: Thomeé, Phys Ther 1997; Silbernagel et al., Am J Sports Med 2007</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E42** (grade A (statement)). AHA scientific statement (2023): resistance training is recommended for adults with and without cardiovascular disease. It lowers blood pressure and improves glucose control and function. Avoid breath-holding (Valsalva). People with CVD should get individualized clearance.

<p class="src">Source: Paluch et al., Circulation 2024 — https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001189</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E43** (grade A (guideline)). Pre-exercise screening (ACSM 2015): anyone with symptoms of cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease (chest pain, unusual breathlessness, fainting) should get medical clearance before starting. Otherwise, light-to-moderate exercise can begin and progress.

<p class="src">Source: Riebe et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2015 (known literature)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E45** (grade B (known literature)). Getting-up-from-the-floor strategies can be taught to older adults. Practice it before you ever need it (backward chaining: kneel → half-kneel → stand, using sturdy furniture).

<p class="src">Source: Hofmeyer et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 2002 (floor-rise strategy training)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E46** (grade A− (meta, known literature)). Orthostatic hypotension (a blood-pressure drop on standing) is common in older adults. A meta-analysis found it in about 22% of community-dwelling older people. The risk is higher with some blood-pressure and other medicines. Practical rule: sit, pump your ankles, then stand slowly while holding something.

<p class="src">Source: Saedon et al., J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2020 (prevalence of orthostatic hypotension, systematic review & meta-analysis)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E47** (grade D (physiology)). The calf muscle pump: calf contraction compresses the deep veins and, with the venous valves, pushes blood back toward the heart. It's standard physiology. Walking and heel raises activate it. A red flag is one swollen, red, painful calf (possible clot), which needs a doctor, not exercise.

<p class="src">Source: Standard physiology texts; e.g. Recek, Int J Angiol 2013 "Calf pump activity influencing venous hemodynamics in the lower extremity" (known literature)</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E50** (grade A (tool)). CDC STEADI 4-Stage Balance Test: feet side by side, semi-tandem (instep beside big toe), tandem (heel to toe), one leg; up to 10 s each, stop at the first stage not held. The CDC uses the tandem stand as a screening checkpoint: under 10 s is worth discussing with a clinician.

<p class="src">Source: CDC STEADI — opened https://www.cdc.gov/steadi/media/pdfs/STEADI-Assessment-4Stage-508.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E59** (grade A (Cochrane, low certainty)). Exercise for hand osteoarthritis (Cochrane): 7 trials, 534 people, mostly women. After a hand-exercise programme, pain was 0.5 points lower (0–10), function 2.2 points better (0–36) and finger stiffness 0.7 points lower (0–10). Small effects, low or very low certainty, not sustained at medium- and long-term follow-up. The few adverse events were more finger-joint inflammation and hand pain. Say "may help a little with stiffness and hand use", never "fixes arthritis".

<p class="src">Source: Østerås et al., Cochrane 2017 — opened https://www.cochrane.org/CD010388/MUSKEL_exercise-hand-osteoarthritis</p>

</div>
